The table brings together the tools for describing **nominal**, **ordinal**, and [**interval variable**]{.important-text}s across all three tutorials. Everything that follows explains why the entries differ and how to produce them in R.

Interval variables give you a wider set of descriptive tools because their values are ordered and the distances between values are meaningful. The same three dimensions apply at every level of measurement --- central tendency, dispersion, and shape --- but the tools available depend on what the values actually mean. The median requires a meaningful rank order, so it is not appropriate for nominal variables. The mean assumes equal intervals between values, so it is not appropriate for ordinal variables. Interval variables permit the mean in addition to the median and mode, though the mode is rarely informative for precisely measured data.

- [**Central tendency**]{.important-text} for interval variables is described by the **median** and [**mean**]{.important-text}, computed with `median()` and `mean()`, adding `na.rm = TRUE` when the variable has missing values. The mode is almost never useful for interval data because values are often measured so precisely that no single value repeats very often. The median is the value at the 50th percentile and is robust to [**outliers**]{.important-text}. The mean is the arithmetic average and can be pulled away from the center by extreme values. When the distribution is roughly [**symmetric**]{.important-text}, the two are similar. When they diverge, inspect the distribution for skew or outliers. In a strongly [**skewed**]{.important-text} distribution the median often better represents a typical case, because it is not pulled by extreme values.

- [**Dispersion**]{.important-text} for interval variables is captured by the [**range**]{.important-text} (`range()`), [**percentile**]{.important-text}s (`quantile()`), and [**standard deviation**]{.important-text} (`sd()`). The [**interquartile range**]{.important-text}, or [**IQR**]{.important-text}, is the distance from the 25th to the 75th percentile; it describes the middle half of the data and is less affected by outliers than the full range. The standard deviation is the typical distance of observations from the mean, in the original units of the variable; the [**variance**]{.important-text} is its square, in squared units, which is why the standard deviation is the one you report. One important caution: standard deviations are only comparable within a variable or across samples of the same variable.

- The [**shape of the distribution**]{.important-text} of an interval variable is best assessed visually. A [**histogram**]{.important-text} (`geom_histogram()`) groups values into bins and shows the overall pattern of the distribution --- its center, spread, symmetry or skew, and whether it is [**unimodal**]{.important-text}, [**bimodal**]{.important-text}, or uniform. The `bins` and `binwidth` arguments affect how much detail you see. A [**box plot**]{.important-text} (`geom_boxplot()`) summarizes the median, IQR, and outliers in a compact form that becomes especially useful when comparing distributions across groups. When reading either plot, ask: where is the center, how spread out are the values, is the distribution symmetric or skewed, and are there outliers?

In R, load [dplyr]{.package-name} and [ggplot2]{.package-name} once at the top of your script or Quarto document with `library(dplyr)` and `library(ggplot2)` before any code that uses functions from those packages. The analysis tools introduced in this tutorial are `median()`, `mean()`, `range()`, `min()`, `max()`, `quantile()`, and `sd()` --- all take the variable as their first argument, and `na.rm = TRUE` as a second when the variable has missing values.

For visualization, histograms and box plots follow the same layered ggplot structure as bar charts. When a plotted interval variable has missing values, filter those cases before passing the data to `ggplot()` --- otherwise ggplot prints a warning that would appear in a knitted document.

- **Histograms:** Use `geom_histogram()` in place of `geom_bar()`, with `fill` to set the bar color, `color = "white"` to add bar outlines, and `bins` or `binwidth` to control bin size.

- **Reference lines:** Use `geom_vline()` to mark a statistic. Inside `aes()`, bare variable names work: `aes(xintercept = median(wage_growth, na.rm = TRUE))`. Outside `aes()`, use the full `data$variable` syntax. Fixed settings like `color` and `linetype` always go outside `aes()`. To label the line, add `annotate("text", x = ..., y = ..., label = ...)` --- use `counties$variable` inside `annotate()` since it does not inherit the data context from `ggplot()`.

- **Box plots:** Map the variable to `y` rather than `x`, use `geom_boxplot()`, and set `x = ""` to suppress the unnecessary x-axis category label.

Which summaries should you present? Report the mean or median and the standard deviation or IQR, or show a histogram or box plot --- but do not bury your reader in every statistic and every graph just because you can. Tables and plots often communicate overlapping information, so choose the display that best serves your purpose rather than presenting both automatically. Whatever you choose, describe its important features in the text --- do not leave a table or figure to speak for itself. The goal is always to give readers enough to see the center, spread, and shape of the distribution.

Tutorial 7 turns from one variable to two. The question changes from what a variable looks like on its own to whether two variables are related, and the level of measurement continues to decide which tools apply --- now for both variables at once.
